description: Reviewed research added by Brali Research Watch on 2026-08-28. The established wakeful-rest protocol already has a reviewed 2026 meta-analysis; this batch adds a same-year ecological challenge study so Brali does not generalize declarative-memory evidence to complex educational reading.

research_candidates.title: Wakeful rest and memory consolidation in an ecologically valid educational setting: no benefit over distractor tasks
research_candidates.review_notes: Full open-access article reviewed. In a randomized classroom study, 161 university students read an expository text and were assigned to eight minutes of wakeful rest, social media, math problems, or a content-similar reading task. Immediate and one-week tests measured factual recall and conceptual understanding. Wakeful rest did not show a consistent advantage over the distractor conditions. This is an important boundary for Brali: the existing meta-analytic support for wakeful rest concerns declarative-memory paradigms and should not be presented as proof that quiet rest improves comprehension or retention of complex educational material.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Wakeful rest and memory consolidation in an ecologically valid educational setting: no benefit over distractor tasks
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Seban P, Šikl R, Prošek T, Urban K. Psychological Research. 2026;90:42.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Randomized four-group classroom study. University students read an expository text for eight minutes and were then assigned to eight minutes of wakeful rest, social-media use, math problems or a content-similar interference text. They completed an immediate test and a different but conceptually aligned test one week later.
evidence_decisions.population: 161 university students tested in a supervised classroom setting.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Eight minutes of guided wakeful rest based on an autogenic-training procedure, compared with eight minutes of social-media use, math problems or reading a content-similar interference text after learning an expository passage.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: The existing Brali wakeful-rest protocol must not promise better comprehension or long-term retention for complex educational reading. In this more ecologically valid randomized study, eight minutes of post-reading wakeful rest did not produce a consistent advantage over social media, math or similar-text reading on immediate or one-week factual and conceptual tests. Keep the protocol narrow: it is an optional declarative-memory tactic, not a general learning upgrade.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: This single study proves that wakeful rest never helps learning.
Social-media use immediately after learning is harmless in every setting.
All post-learning distractor tasks are equivalent.
Autogenic training or guided rest is ineffective for every outcome.
The null classroom result cancels the broader declarative-memory meta-analysis.
The findings generalize unchanged beyond university students and the specific expository material tested.
limitations: The study used one expository learning task in a university-student population.
The wakeful-rest condition used an autogenic-training implementation and therefore does not represent every possible quiet-rest procedure.
Only one eight-minute post-learning duration was tested.
The delayed test used different but conceptually aligned questions rather than identical items from the immediate test.
A single null study cannot establish absence of a wakeful-rest effect across all complex learning tasks or populations.
evidence_decisions.notes: Evidence role: explicit boundary for the existing reviewed protocol and public copy. State that laboratory/meta-analytic declarative-memory effects do not yet translate cleanly to comprehension of complex educational material. Prefer recall-sensitive use cases and keep active learning methods primary.
